clinical_knowledge.topic: Contrast-Induced Acute Kidney Injury (Acute Tubular Necrosis) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Contrast-Induced Acute Kidney Injury (Acute Tubular Necrosis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Discontinue nephrotoxic agents (hold Lisinopril/NSAIDs), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: decreased urine output and rising creatinine after contrast CT scan

Key HPI features: 64M with baseline chronic kidney disease stage 3 (creatinine 1.6 mg/dL) underwent contrast-enhanced CT angiography of lower extremities for claudication 48 hours ago. Now reports oligarchic urine output (<300 mL/day), peripheral ankle puffiness, and general malaise.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Mild bilateral pedal edema. Bloods: Serum Creatinine jumped from baseline 1.6 to 3.4 mg/dL; BUN 54 mg/dL; K+ 5.1 mEq/L. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells, FENA > 2% consistent with acute tubular necrosis (ATN).
Relevant background/PMH: CKD stage 3a (baseline eGFR 45), hypertension, peripheral artery disease
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Contrast-Induced Acute Kidney Injury (Acute Tubular Necrosis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Prerenal AKI from dehydration without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Anuria (no urine output at all) — suggests a more severe or different process.
management_principles: Provide isotonic IV crystalloid hydration (0.9% NaCl)
Monitor strict intake/output, daily electrolytes, and acid-base status
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 64M with baseline CKD stage 3 presenting with acute kidney injury (oliguria, creatinine spike) 48 hours post-iodinated contrast exposure.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Mild bilateral pedal edema. Bloods: Serum Creatinine jumped from baseline 1.6 to 3.4 mg/dL; BUN 54 mg/dL; K+ 5.1 mEq/L. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells, FENA > 2% consistent with acute tubular necrosis (ATN).
reference_soap.assessment: Contrast-Induced Acute Kidney Injury (CI-AKI) manifesting as Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN).
reference_soap.plan: Discontinue nephrotoxic agents (hold Lisinopril/NSAIDs). Provide isotonic IV crystalloid hydration (0.9% NaCl). Monitor strict intake/output, daily electrolytes, and acid-base status. Avoid repeat contrast exposures. Supportive care; prognosis good for recovery within 7-14 days.

learning_objectives: Identify risk factors for contrast-induced acute kidney injury (baseline CKD, diabetes, volume depletion)
Interpret urine microscopy and fractional excretion of sodium (FENA > 2%, muddy brown casts) in ATN
Implement evidence-based preventive volume expansion protocols prior to contrast procedures
Formulate supportive inpatient care and nephrotoxin avoidance strategies during acute renal failure

teaching.diagnosis: Contrast-Induced Acute Kidney Injury (Acute Tubular Necrosis)
teaching.one_liner: IV contrast dye can directly injure kidney tubules in patients with reduced baseline kidney function, causing a rise in creatinine and reduced urine output 24-72 hours after the scan.
red_flags: Anuria (no urine output at all) — suggests a more severe or different process

must_ask.objective: Timing relative to the contrast scan
must_ask.say: When did you have the CT scan with dye, and when did the swelling and low urine start?
How much urine have you been passing compared to normal?
Did you know you had kidney problems before this scan?

must_ask.objective: Medications around the time of the scan
must_ask.say: Were you taking any blood pressure pills or pain relievers around the time of the scan?
Where is the swelling, and how has your energy been?
